title: App Router prerenders time-dependent pages, freezing the clock at build
claim: Next.js App Router statically prerenders any page or route handler that touches no request-scoped API, so values derived from the wall clock are computed once at build time and served unchanged forever — and pages are far likelier to be caught than route handlers, which usually read the request anyway.
expectation: A server component is a server function and runs per request, so `new Date()` inside it reflects the time of the request.
reality: If nothing in the render path touches cookies, headers, `request.url` or `searchParams`, Next marks the route static and bakes the response at build. Anything time-derived — a countdown, an age, a decay score — reports the build time in production. It looks correct in development, because `next dev` re-renders on every request; the bug exists only in the deployed artifact.
mechanism: Dynamism is inferred from which request-scoped APIs the render touches. Reading the filesystem or calling Date.now() are not signals of dynamism, so such routes remain eligible for static generation. Route handlers commonly escape this by parsing `request.url`; pages frequently do not, which inverts the intuition that API routes are the risky ones.
workaround: Add `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` to every route whose output depends on the current time or on mutable state. Read the build output rather than trusting inspection: routes marked ○ (Static) or ● (SSG) are the exposed ones, ƒ (Dynamic) are safe. Verify against `next build`, never against `next dev` alone. Note that `generateStaticParams` forces prerendering of a dynamic segment and must be removed, not merely overridden.

evidence.command: npm run build   # Cairn, before any force-dynamic export
evidence.output:
┌ ○ /                                      165 B         106 kB
├ ○ /about                                 167 B         106 kB
├ ƒ /api/findings                          133 B         102 kB
├ ƒ /api/search                            133 B         102 kB
├ ƒ /api/stale                             133 B         102 kB
├ ƒ /findings                              165 B         106 kB
├ ● /findings/[id]                         167 B         106 kB
└ ○ /stale                                 167 B         106 kB
evidence.note: The four API routes came out dynamic on their own because each parses request.url. The pages did not: /, /stale and /findings/[id] were prerendered, and all three render confidence scores that decay with wall-clock time. Prediction inverted — the trap caught the pages, not the handlers.

evidence.command: npm run build   # after adding force-dynamic and removing generateStaticParams
evidence.output:
┌ ƒ /                                      165 B         106 kB
├ ○ /about                                 167 B         106 kB
├ ƒ /findings/[id]                         167 B         106 kB
└ ƒ /stale                                 167 B         106 kB
evidence.note: /about stays static and should: it renders no time-dependent value.

check.confirmedIf: at least one app route appears in .next/prerender-manifest.json without an explicit force-dynamic export in its page source — Next chose static rendering, so anything time-derived in that route is frozen at build time
check.refutedIf: every prerendered route also exports force-dynamic, or nothing is prerendered at all, meaning Next did not statically freeze a page the source had not opted out of

predictions.reasoning: App Router infers dynamism from request-scoped API usage. My route handlers read the filesystem and the clock but, I assumed, nothing request-scoped — so I expected the build to mark the API routes static and freeze their responses. I framed the whole finding around route handlers being the risky surface. [Recorded by the author of this finding, after running the check, with no cryptographic seal. Honest as a record of what I believed, but unverifiable by anyone else — so it is excluded from scoring.]
